content:
What we can be sure of is that Apple will raise prices when it unveils the iPhone 18 Pro next month. Apple previously raised prices across the board due to rising memory costs, but at the time it did not simultaneously increase the prices of existing iPhone models — but that was only a temporary reprieve.

However, two sources now indicate that this year's Pro models will start at $1,399 — even I find it hard to believe Apple would really push the price up that far…

Don't get me wrong: Apple has made it very clear it wants to protect its profit margins, and has never been shy about raising prices significantly. For example, the base-model MacBook Air went from $1,099 to $1,299, a $200 increase. Even the MacBook Neo, which initially surprised everyone with a $599 starting price, has already gone up by $100.

But a $300 increase on the iPhone Pro starting price is outrageous. An increase of that magnitude has historically been reserved for far more expensive products.

Among products that have received $300 price hikes, the cheapest was the base-model MacBook Pro, which went from $1,699 to $1,999. That increase is indeed significant, nearly 18%. But a $300 hike over the previous generation for the iPhone 18 Pro would amount to a 27% increase.

The most upvoted comment comes from IndomitableSlake

Apple will charge whatever it wants, and consumers will keep paying. The housing, auto, and appliance industries have already proven that. What difference does it make? People will just take on more debt. 120 years of social and economic history have proven that long-term debt brings absolutely no consequences; let's just go borrow some more money.

Again, this price hike is not entirely impossible. For example, the prices of some upgraded MacBook configurations have indeed doubled; Apple certainly does love making money. But Tim Cook did hint on an earnings call that the company would not protect its margins at all costs.

As for sales, I do think this price increase will give many people pause about upgrading, especially knowing that next year's Pro models look set to be an even bigger upgrade.

Of course, the counterargument is that the Apple Upgrade Program can ease some of the pressure. Some people might feel fine with leasing an iPhone 18 Pro for a year and then upgrading to the 20th-anniversary edition next year. But for those who choose to buy outright, a price hike of this magnitude will be a major deterrent.

What do you think? Do you feel a $300 increase is reasonable, or is a 27% hike too much for Apple? Feel free to share your views in the comments section.
